Biology

 Home
OurBigBook.com Words: 182k Articles: 6k
Biology studies living systems: how biological cells maintain themselves, how organisms develop and reproduce, and how evolution generates diversity. Its scales connect molecules, genes, biological cells, organisms and the interactions studied by ecology. These are complementary viewpoints: a protein's chemistry can explain a cellular mechanism, while evolution explains why inherited variants of that mechanism persist. See Clark, Douglas and Choi, Biology 2e: the science of biology.
Two organizing ideas make this immense subject navigable: shared cellular organization and descent with inherited modification. A neuron and a gliding bacterium differ dramatically in shape and behavior, yet both depend on a cell membrane and metabolism. Their differences become intelligible through specialization and evolution.
Keep observations separate from the mathematical models used to explain them. A measured membrane potential is evidence; an idealized two-state ion-channel gating equation proposes a mechanism. A mathematical model earns trust through predictions and comparisons with measurements. Its assumptions delimit its usefulness, and disagreement can reveal missing biology rather than a faulty measurement.

Centrifugation

Words: 2k Articles: 18
Biology OurBigBook.com
Centrifugation separates suspended material by its motion relative to a rotating liquid. A centrifuge rotor creates an outward centrifugal acceleration in the rotating reference frame; material denser than its surroundings tends to move outward, opposed by drag force. Collected material can form a centrifugation pellet, leaving a supernatant, or remain in separated zones within a density gradient. The useful question is which physical difference the separation exploits: a difference in sedimentation coefficient or a difference in buoyant density.
Centrifugation makes otherwise slow settling useful for studying biological cells, organelles, proteins and DNA. Separation and identification are different steps: a centrifugation pellet is a collected fraction, not proof that it contains only one kind of organelle. The lysozyme wall-removal experiment illustrates a complementary readout: testing material released into the separated liquid can be more informative than inspecting the retained solids.

Analytical ultracentrifugation (AUC)

Words: 218 Articles: 1
Centrifugation OurBigBook.com
Analytical ultracentrifugation observes concentration profiles during rotation, rather than only recovering a separated pellet. Sector-shaped sample cells rotate past optical detectors. Absorbance scans measure attenuation at selected radii. A Rayleigh interferometer compares a sample sector with a solvent reference, converting concentration-dependent refractive-index changes into fringe shifts. Repeating scans follows a sedimentation boundary or the approach to a stationary distribution.[ref]
For a dilute solute of buoyant mass mb​ and translational friction fh​, radial force balance gives s=mb​/fh​, where s is the sedimentation coefficient. Diffusion supplies D=kB​T/fh​. A velocity experiment resolves boundary motion and broadening; a sedimentation equilibrium experiment instead measures dlnc/d(r2)=mb​ω2/(2kB​T). This follows from the Boltzmann distribution in centrifugal potential −mb​ω2r2/2. The two approaches separate frictional size information from buoyant mass information; shape, hydration and solvent properties must be specified to infer a unique geometric dimension.

Molar mass from sedimentation and diffusion (M=Rgas​Ts/[D(1−vˉρs​)])

Words: 76
Analytical ultracentrifugation OurBigBook.com
Let M be molar mass in kgmol−1, vˉ partial specific volume, ρs​ solvent density, and NA​ the Avogadro constant. The buoyant molecular mass is mb​=M(1−vˉρs​)/NA​. Combining sedimentation coefficient s=mb​/fh​ and the thermal diffusion-friction relation D=kB​T/fh​ eliminates the unknown friction and proves the displayed formula, with Rgas​=NA​kB​. Once friction is known, Rh​=fh​/(6πη) defines a hydrodynamic radius using Stokes's law. Mass and radius are different inferences: an extended molecule need not occupy the volume of that friction-equivalent sphere.

Microcentrifuge

Words: 16
Centrifugation OurBigBook.com
A microcentrifuge performs centrifugation of small sample tubes, as used to concentrate biological cells and separate debris in the PV92 teaching experiment.

Centrifuge rotor

Words: 311 Articles: 2
Centrifugation OurBigBook.com
A centrifuge rotor holds sample vessels around the rotation axis. A fixed-angle centrifuge rotor holds tubes at a fixed inclination; a swinging-bucket centrifuge rotor lets them swing outward during rotation. Material moves away from the axis, so a centrifugation pellet can first collect against an outer tube wall rather than travel along the entire tube axis. Geometry sets both the rotor radius and the travel distance.[ref]

Rotor radius (r)

Words: 52
Centrifuge rotor OurBigBook.com
The rotor radius r is the perpendicular distance from the rotation axis to a specified sample position, not the tube's length. A filled tube spans a range rmin​≤r≤rmax​. Consequently, one rotational speed produces different local centrifugal accelerations along that range. A reported relative centrifugal force needs a stated reference position, such as the outermost sample radius.

Relative centrifugal force (RCF=a/g0​)

Words: 185
Centrifuge rotor OurBigBook.com
Relative centrifugal force is the dimensionless ratio of the local centrifugal acceleration magnitude a to the conventional gravitational reference g0​=9.80665ms−2. Despite its name, it is an acceleration ratio: the actual force on a specified mass m is ma. With angular speed ω and rotor radius r, a=ω2r. If n is the numerical rotational speed in revolutions per minute and rcm​ the numerical rotor radius in centimetres, unit conversion gives
ω=602πn​s−1,RCF=9.80665(rcm​/100)(2πn/60)2​≃1.118×10−5rcm​n2.
(1)
Thus rpm alone does not specify the centrifugal acceleration.[ref]
For a stipulated 3000rpm, rotor radii of 5 and 10cm give approximately 503 and 1006 times g0​. Doubling the rotor radius doubles relative centrifugal force; doubling rpm quadruples it. Even equal relative centrifugal forces do not guarantee equal separation: travel distance, elapsed time, viscosity, sample density and particle shape still matter. These are comparisons of a mathematical model, not instructions for running an instrument.

Centrifugation pellet

Words: 24
Centrifugation OurBigBook.com
A centrifugation pellet is material accumulated against the vessel wall by centrifugation. Its existence establishes collection, not purity; other suspended material can be trapped or co-sediment.

Supernatant

Words: 30
Centrifugation OurBigBook.com
A supernatant is the liquid remaining above settled or pelleted material. It can contain dissolved molecules and particles that have not reached the centrifugation pellet; a visually clear supernatant need not be chemically empty.

Sedimentation coefficient (s=v/(ω2r))

Words: 187
Centrifugation OurBigBook.com
The sedimentation coefficient s is radial drift velocity divided by local centrifugal acceleration. It has units of time and combines particle properties with those of the surrounding liquid. In a dilute, deterministic mathematical model with negligible particle inertia, an effective displaced volume V, particle mass m, local liquid density ρf​ and linear friction coefficient f>0 give
fv=(m−ρf​V)ω2r,s=ω2rv​=fm−ρf​V​.
(2)
The subtraction represents buoyancy. Equal mass does not imply equal s: changing shape changes drag force, and changing the medium changes both buoyancy and viscosity.[ref]
For an isolated sphere of radius b and uniform density ρp​, Stokes's law supplies f=6πηb, where η is dynamic viscosity, and m=(4π/3)b3ρp​. Therefore
s=9η2b2(ρp​−ρf​)​.
(3)
This original force-balance check predicts fourfold s on doubling b with everything else fixed, and zero drift when ρp​=ρf​. It applies to dilute isolated spheres in Stokes flow, not arbitrary folded proteins or crowded suspensions. If s and ω remain constant in a uniform medium, the ordinary differential equation dr/dt=sω2r has the exponential function solution r(t)=r(0)esω2t. Arrival at an outer boundary therefore depends on starting position as well as s; a separation has no universal size cutoff.

Differential centrifugation

Words: 60
Centrifugation OurBigBook.com
Differential centrifugation successively separates centrifugation pellets from supernatants by differences in settling rate. A first centrifugation pellet can enrich faster-settling material; a later centrifugation pellet from its supernatant can enrich slower-settling material. The fractions overlap because particles have different starting positions and can become trapped. Differential centrifugation is consequently an enrichment method, not automatic identification or complete purification.[ref]

Density-gradient centrifugation

Words: 1k Articles: 7
Centrifugation OurBigBook.com
Density-gradient centrifugation uses a liquid whose density varies along the separation direction. A band does not by itself establish which mechanism produced it: rate-zonal centrifugation separates by migration rate before equilibrium, whereas isopycnic centrifugation uses equilibrium positions set by buoyant density.
The distinction is between a moving clock and a restoring balance. In rate-zonal centrifugation, two species may occupy different positions because their sedimentation coefficients differ, even when their buoyant densities agree. In isopycnic centrifugation, two differently sized species can converge to the same band because their buoyant densities agree. Conversely, equal mass does not ensure equal migration velocity: shape affects drag force, and medium density affects buoyancy.[ref]
The worked finite-time rate-zonal separation and linear-gradient isopycnic focusing examples isolate these mechanisms in chosen mathematical models. The actual DNA experiment described under isopycnic centrifugation illustrates the second mechanism; its initial collection of biological cells into centrifugation pellets is a different operation from the later molecular banding. Collecting liquid fractions from a tube can recover material at different positions, but the position alone does not identify its molecules or establish purity.

Density-gradient flotation

Words: 35
Density-gradient centrifugation OurBigBook.com
Separation in which a particle's buoyant properties cause it to move toward a lower-density part of a gradient. A liposome fraction can thereby be separated from unassociated soluble proteins; copurification alone does not demonstrate correct membrane topology.

Isopycnic centrifugation

Words: 737 Articles: 3
Density-gradient centrifugation OurBigBook.com
In isopycnic centrifugation, a species concentrates near the position where the liquid's density matches its buoyant density. In a density gradient increasing outward, material displaced inward encounters less-dense liquid and tends to move outward; material displaced outward encounters denser liquid and tends to move inward. Diffusion broadens the resulting band. If the density gradient never reaches the species' buoyant density, a matching equilibrium position need not exist within the vessel.[ref]
The 1958 paper The replication of DNA in Escherichia coli by Matthew Meselson and Franklin W. Stahl (pp. 672–676, Figures 1–4) makes the distinction concrete. Its separation apparatus was a Spinco Model E ultracentrifuge with an Escherichia coli lysate in a cesium chloride density gradient. Ultraviolet wave absorption photographs of the rotating sample were scanned with a recording microdensitometer: peak position reported buoyant density, while signal above baseline reported DNA concentration.[ref]
Cultures received labeled nitrogen; chilled biological cells were collected as centrifugation pellets and disrupted before molecular banding.[ref]
Mixed lysates labeled fully with the nitrogen isotope 15N and unlabeled lysates supplied reference bands; a mixture including intermediate material checked its position relative to those references. Figure 1 followed band formation over time, helping distinguish a migrating distribution from an approximately stationary one. These controls address resolution, calibration and approach to equilibrium. They do not make every ultraviolet-absorbing component identifiable as DNA, or turn a band into a direct image of individual strands. The DNA replication article develops the copying inference; here the key result is a separation by buoyant density, not a claim that heavier-labeled DNA is physically larger.[ref]
Linear-gradient isopycnic focusing (z∗​=(ρb​−ρ0​)/G)
Words: 364
Isopycnic centrifugation OurBigBook.com
Why does an isopycnic centrifugation band return after displacement? Choose a dilute mathematical model with outward coordinate z, constant local centrifugal acceleration a>0, fixed displaced volume V>0, linear friction coefficient f>0, and an imposed liquid density ρf​(z)=ρ0​+Gz with G>0. Treat the species' buoyant density ρb​ as constant in this medium. The sedimentation coefficient force balance gives the ordinary differential equation
dtdz​=fVa​(ρb​−ρf​(z))=−k(z−z∗​),k=fVaG​,z∗​=Gρb​−ρ0​​.
(4)
Its exponential function solution is z(t)=z∗​+(z(0)−z∗​)e−kt. The sign of the velocity reverses across z∗​, proving stable equilibrium when z∗​ lies inside the liquid. Changing V/f changes the approach time 1/k, while z∗​ depends on buoyant density and the imposed density gradient. A real centrifuge rotor has radially varying centrifugal acceleration; the constant-a approximation describes a short radial interval. Here the density gradient is held fixed, rather than modeling its formation.
For an original dimensionless example, let u=z/L and τ=t/T, where L is column length and T a chosen time scale. Write q=z∗​/L and λ=kT, so u(τ)=q+(u(0)−q)e−λτ. Species A and B have the same q=0.45 but different friction-dependent rates: (λA​,uA​(0))=(0.4,0.1) and (λB​,uB​(0))=(1.6,0.95). A moves outward and B inward, both toward u=0.45. Species C has (qC​,λC​,uC​(0))=(0.8,0.8,0.1) and approaches a separate band at u=0.8. At τ=4, their positions are approximately 0.3793, 0.4508 and 0.7715: a finite-time photograph would still show A short of its limiting position.
An equilibrium band has finite width because diffusion opposes focusing. In the same local model, let c(z) be concentration and let the constant diffusion coefficient be D>0. Combining the restoring drift with Fick's laws, zero net flux requires
J=−k(z−z∗​)c−Ddzdc​=0,c(z)=c(z∗​)exp[−2Dk(z−z∗​)2​].
(5)
Dividing by c and integrating proves the Gaussian function profile, whose standard deviation is σz​=D/k​. This local result assumes that the band is narrow relative to its distance from the boundaries and that D, k and the density gradient vary negligibly across it. Equal buoyant densities therefore imply coincident centers in this model, not identical widths. A band outside the available density range has no such interior restoring point.
Buoyant density (ρb​)
Words: 59
Isopycnic centrifugation OurBigBook.com
Buoyant density is the surrounding liquid density at which a species has no net centrifugal drift under the stated conditions. It depends on interactions with the medium, including associated solvent, rather than necessarily equaling the dry substance's density. Equal buoyant densities can give overlapping bands even for differently sized proteins or DNA fragments.[ref]
Cesium chloride density gradient
Words: 33
Isopycnic centrifugation OurBigBook.com
A cesium chloride density gradient forms when the salt CsCl redistributes in a rotating chemical solution. It can supply matching-density positions for DNA during isopycnic centrifugation.[ref]

Rate-zonal centrifugation

Words: 454 Articles: 1
Density-gradient centrifugation OurBigBook.com
Rate-zonal centrifugation resolves an initially narrow sample zone by differences in sedimentation coefficient during a finite interval. Its bands remain transient: extending the interval can carry material into a centrifugation pellet. Thus a density gradient need not imply an equilibrium buoyant density measurement.[ref]
A typical preparation layers a narrow sample above a preformed density gradient, often containing sucrose. The initial zone must be narrow enough that differences in starting position do not overwhelm the later separation. The run ends while useful bands remain inside the liquid. In the simple case where all particles are denser than every part of the column, none has an interior isopycnic centrifugation position.[ref][ref]
The sedimentation coefficient s=(m−ρf​V)/f explains why separation is not an ordering by mass alone. At fixed local centrifugal acceleration, increasing displaced volume can increase buoyancy, while a less compact shape can increase the linear friction coefficient and reduce velocity. Even for a sphere, Stokes's law gives s=2b2(ρp​−ρf​)/(9η), so both the density difference and the dynamic viscosity matter. The resulting sedimentation coefficient can change along a density gradient.
Finite-time rate-zonal separation
Words: 267
Rate-zonal centrifugation OurBigBook.com
Consider two dilute populations of spheres with the same buoyant density and radii b and 2b. Adopt the fixed linear density gradient and constant local centrifugal acceleration of linear-gradient isopycnic focusing, with constant dynamic viscosity and negligible diffusion. Stokes's law makes V/f proportional to b2, so doubling radius multiplies the migration rate parameter by four, although the mass increases eightfold.
Use u=z/L, τ=t/T and q=(ρb​−ρ0​)/(GL)=2. The liquid occupies 0≤u≤1, so the matching density position lies beyond its outer boundary. Both populations begin at u(0)=0.1; choose λA​=0.15 and λB​=0.6. Their band-center trajectories are
uA​(τ)=2−1.9e−0.15τ,uB​(τ)=2−1.9e−0.6τ.
(6)
At τ=0.5, they lie at approximately 0.2373 and 0.5924; at τ=1, at 0.3647 and 0.9573. Equal buoyant density has not prevented a useful finite-time separation. Solving uB​(τ)=1 using the natural logarithm gives first boundary arrival at τ=ln(1.9)/0.6≃1.0698. The corresponding arrival for A is ln(1.9)/0.15≃4.2790. Trajectories describe migration only until contact with the boundary; subsequent collection into a centrifugation pellet is not represented by extending the curve beyond u=1.
This is the useful contrast with isopycnic centrifugation: stopping time helps determine the recovered positions in rate-zonal centrifugation, whereas a stationary matching density position sets the limiting band center in isopycnic centrifugation. Real resolution also depends on initial zone width, diffusion and variations in particle properties; distinct calculated centers alone do not prove that fractions will be pure.

Förster resonance energy transfer

Words: 2k Articles: 13
Biophysical measurement OurBigBook.com
Förster resonance energy transfer is a nonradiative transfer of energy from an excited state of a FRET donor to a nearby FRET acceptor, through coupling of their electric dipoles. The transfer step does not emit a photon that the FRET acceptor subsequently absorbs. It competes with the FRET donor's own fluorescence and other routes out of its excited state. A fluorescent FRET acceptor can then emit fluorescence; an absorbing but nonfluorescent FRET acceptor can still receive the transferred energy.[ref]
The striking use of FRET is to turn a change in molecular proximity into an optical readout. Proteins carrying a FRET donor and a FRET acceptor may change the readout when they associate, as in the chemotaxis FRET assay; two labels on one protein may report a change in its shape. Interpretation depends on the FRET spectral overlap, FRET dipole orientation factor and labeling geometry, as well as separation. A change in FRET is therefore evidence about proximity under specified conditions, rather than a direct measurement of an arbitrary distance.[ref]
For a single pair with fixed Förster distance R0​ and label separation r, the FRET efficiency is
E=1+(r/R0​)61​.
(7)
At r=R0​, half the FRET donor excitations transfer energy. At r=R0​/2, the model gives E=64/65≈98.46%; at r=2R0​, it gives E=1/65≈1.54%. The sixth power makes FRET especially useful near the Förster distance, with little sensitivity to further separation once transfer is already negligible. These are model calculations, not measurements of a particular pair.

Single-molecule Förster resonance energy transfer

Words: 26
Förster resonance energy transfer OurBigBook.com
single-molecule Förster resonance energy transfer records energy-transfer signals from individual donor–acceptor pairs. State occupancies and dwell times can constrain structural dynamics, provided dye photophysics, labeling geometry and time resolution are controlled.

FRET donor

Words: 37
Förster resonance energy transfer OurBigBook.com
A FRET donor supplies the initial excited state energy. Its fluorescence provides both an emission channel and a reference FRET donor lifetime when no FRET acceptor is present. Calling a label a FRET donor describes its role in a chosen pair, rather than a permanent classification of the molecule.

FRET acceptor

Words: 20
Förster resonance energy transfer OurBigBook.com
A FRET acceptor receives the excited state energy. Its absorption must support FRET spectral overlap with the FRET donor. FRET sensitized emission requires a fluorescent FRET acceptor; measuring a shortened FRET donor lifetime does not.

Förster resonance energy transfer OurBigBook.com
FRET efficiency is the probability that an excitation of the FRET donor ends in transfer to the FRET acceptor. Write kD​=kr​+knr​ for the total decay rate without a FRET acceptor, including radiative fluorescence and other decay, and kT​ for the transfer rate. For constant competing rates,
kT​=kD​(rR0​​)6,E=kD​+kT​kT​​=∫0∞​kT​e−(kD​+kT​)tdt.
(8)
The integral counts transfer events among all excitations in a population with exponential decay. Substitution gives the separation law above. This short rate argument assumes one FRET donor, one FRET acceptor, weak coupling, an available FRET acceptor, and fixed geometry during the decay; it is not a model for arbitrary interacting labels.[ref]
Förster distance (R0​)
Words: 387 Articles: 3
FRET efficiency OurBigBook.com
The Förster distance is the separation giving FRET efficiency E=1/2 for the specified pair and conditions. It is a property of the optical pair and its environment, rather than a universal length. In the usual pair model,
R06​∝κ2QD​Jn−4,
(9)
where κ2 is the FRET dipole orientation factor, QD​ the FRET donor quantum yield, J the FRET spectral overlap integral, and n the medium's refractive index. The omitted proportionality constant depends on the unit convention for J.[ref]
If FRET efficiency is known and those assumptions hold, inversion gives
r=R0​(E−1−1)1/6,dEdlogr​=−6E(1−E)1​.
(10)
The derivative explains why errors become troublesome near E=0 or E=1. An illustrative pair with R0​=4 nanometres and another with R0​=6 nanometres both give E=1/2 at their different Förster distances: knowing FRET efficiency alone does not determine r.
A heterogeneous population adds another ambiguity. In a synthetic example with equal weights per FRET donor excitation, efficiencies 0.1 and 0.9 average to 0.5, but their separations are 91/6R0​ and 9−1/6R0​. Their average separation is approximately 1.068R0​, whereas inverting the average FRET efficiency gives R0​. A measured emission ratio has additional detection weights; it need not equal even this excitation-weighted average. The transferable lesson is that an average readout does not uniquely specify a distribution of molecular separations.
FRET spectral overlap (J)
Words: 57
Förster distance OurBigBook.com
FRET spectral overlap quantifies overlap between the FRET donor's emission and the FRET acceptor's absorption as functions of wavelength λ. With normalized donor emission fD​ and acceptor molar absorption coefficient εA​, one convention is
∫0∞​fD​(λ)dλ=1,J=∫0∞​fD​(λ)εA​(λ)λ4dλ.
(11)
Matching two emission colors is insufficient: the receiving absorption matters.[ref]
FRET dipole orientation factor (κ2)
Words: 96
Förster distance OurBigBook.com
The FRET dipole orientation factor describes the geometry of the two transition electric dipoles relative to their separation. Let μ​D​, μ​A​ and r be their unit vectors. Then
κ2=[μ​D​⋅μ​A​−3(μ​D​⋅r)(μ​A​⋅r)]2,0≤κ2≤4.
(12)
For a separation along z, parallel electric dipoles along z give κ2=4, parallel ones along x give 1, and one along x with the other along y gives 0. Thus rotating a pair can change FRET efficiency without changing its separation.
The familiar value κ2=2/3 requires suitable rapid, independent orientation averaging during the FRET donor lifetime. Random orientations across a population of slowly rotating fluorescent proteins do not establish that dynamic condition. [ref]
FRET donor quantum yield (QD​)
Words: 36
Förster distance OurBigBook.com
The FRET donor quantum yield is the emitted fluorescence photon fraction per absorbed excitation photon, measured without a FRET acceptor. In the constant-rate model used for FRET efficiency, QD​=kr​/(kr​+knr​). Changing the FRET donor quantum yield changes the Förster distance, even if label positions remain fixed.

Words: 158
FRET efficiency OurBigBook.com
The FRET donor lifetime is the mean time spent in the excited state. For the constant-rate model of FRET efficiency,
τD​=kD​1​,τDA​=kD​+kT​1​,E=1−τD​τDA​​.
(13)
After a sufficiently brief excitation pulse, the FRET donor's fluorescence follows exponential decay, I(t)=I(0)e−t/τ. With the illustrative values τD​=4 nanoseconds and τDA​=2 nanoseconds, the inferred FRET efficiency is 1/2. Multiplying I(0) changes brightness without changing this decay time.
The lifetime comparison requires the same nontransfer decay rates in the reference and paired samples. Changes in the FRET donor's environment or a different nonradiative loss can also shorten the FRET donor lifetime. Heterogeneous FRET efficiencies or slowly varying FRET dipole orientation factors need an appropriate decay model; substituting any fitted average lifetime into the single-pair formula can mislead. [ref]

FRET sensitized emission

Words: 247 Articles: 1
Förster resonance energy transfer OurBigBook.com
FRET sensitized emission is FRET acceptor fluorescence caused by transfer from an excited FRET donor. Excite predominantly the FRET donor and collect both emission bands. Reduced FRET donor emission and increased FRET acceptor emission are useful together, but an acceptor-to-donor emission ratio is not automatically the FRET efficiency: brightness, label abundance and channel collection also enter.[ref]
FRET optical crosstalk
Words: 195
FRET sensitized emission OurBigBook.com
FRET optical crosstalk includes FRET donor emission leaking into the FRET acceptor detection band and direct excitation of the FRET acceptor by the nominal FRET donor excitation light. Measure donor-only, acceptor-only and unlabeled preparations with the same fluorescence microscope settings to separate these contributions and background.[ref]
An explicit linear measurement model makes the controls' purpose clear. Let D be background-subtracted donor-band counts under donor excitation, A acceptor-band counts under acceptor excitation, and F acceptor-band counts under donor excitation. Donor-only and acceptor-only preparations determine leakage coefficients a and b. Then
S=F−aD−bA
(14)
is a corrected FRET sensitized emission signal under the assumed linear, fixed optical response. In a synthetic example D=100, A=80, a=0.10, b=0.05 and F=34 give S=20. Even a nontransferring sample would give F=14 from these two contaminants. Correcting that signal still does not convert S into FRET efficiency without a calibration of excitation, yields and detection.
A biological comparison also needs a pairing-negative preparation and a known transferring positive preparation. Match label abundance and localization where possible; changing concentration can change encounter frequency as well as brightness. Check that attaching the labels preserves the protein function being investigated. Otherwise the measurement can faithfully report a perturbation introduced by the labels themselves.

Förster resonance energy transfer OurBigBook.com
In FRET photobleaching controls, selectively destroy the FRET acceptor's ability to absorb and test whether FRET donor fluorescence increases. Under unchanged excitation and detection, complete loss of transfer, and an intact FRET donor,
E=1−ID,after​ID,before​​.
(15)
This is a destructive comparison. Monitor acceptor loss, donor-only samples exposed to the bleaching illumination, and an unbleached reference region or time trace. Incomplete bleaching, donor damage, movement or label replenishment violate the comparison. During ordinary recordings, gradual unequal bleaching can instead produce an apparent change of FRET without a biological change.[ref]

FRET proximity readout experiment

Words: 189
Förster resonance energy transfer OurBigBook.com
In Receptor sensitivity in bacterial chemotaxis by Victor Sourjik and others, Victor Sourjik and Howard C. Berg used a cyan fluorescent tag on CheZ as FRET donor and a yellow tag on CheY as FRET acceptor. Escherichia coli biological cells adhered to a polylysine-coated coverslip in a continuously perfused chamber. A fluorescence microscope excited them with a 442-nanometre laser; split emission bands fed two photon-counting detectors. The yellow/cyan emission ratio fell when attractant was added and rose when it was removed.[ref]
Saturating attractant increased cyan emission by an amount matching selective bleaching of the yellow tag: removing the FRET acceptor supported relief of FRET donor transfer. Strains carrying the tagged pair but lacking other chemotaxis machinery showed no stimulus-dependent emission ratio change. Weak illumination reduced bleaching drift.[ref]
The inference is a change in the population of nearby tagged CheY/CheZ pairs associated with CheY phosphorylation. It neither measures each pair's separation nor directly observes motor motion. The readout also averages many biological cells, and perfusion takes finite time. The pathway interpretation belongs to the chemotaxis FRET assay; the general measurement lesson is that molecular association can alter FRET while the geometry of an individual associated pair stays the same.

Model organism

Words: 896 Articles: 4
Biology OurBigBook.com
A model organism is an organism used to investigate biological processes through accessible, repeatable experiments. Its value combines experimental tractability with a carefully delimited relationship to other organisms. For example, a gene deletion in Saccharomyces cerevisiae can test whether a gene is required for growth under specified conditions; adding another gene can test functional complementation. Such interventions support causal inference more directly than merely noticing that a gene and a phenotype occur together. [ref]
The striking opportunity is to ask two experimentally separate questions: what does this component do here, and which part of that function survives a change of species or conditions? The yeast cross-species complementation experiment makes both questions concrete. Model organism evidence transfer requires specifying the function being compared; a useful model organism need not reproduce every feature of another organism.

Arabidopsis thaliana

Words: 10
Model organism OurBigBook.com
A flowering plant used to investigate genetics, chloroplast function and development.

Experimental tractability

Words: 123
Model organism OurBigBook.com
Experimental tractability is the practical ability to cultivate a system, manipulate the variables of interest, and obtain an interpretable readout with appropriate scientific controls. In Saccharomyces cerevisiae, inexpensive cultivation, accessible haploid and diploid states, and tools for introducing DNA make controlled changes of genotype feasible. A haploid biological strain exposes a changed allele without a second copy at that genetic locus, while crosses and meiosis permit tests of inheritance. [ref]
An accessible readout is not necessarily a direct measurement of the mechanism. Growth of a biological colony integrates many cellular functions. Failure to grow could reflect the intended gene deletion, unsuitable conditions, failed genetic transformation, or another mutation. Matching the genetic background and using scientific controls narrows these alternatives. Ease of doing an experiment and strength of its inference are distinct advantages.

Yeast cross-species complementation experiment

Words: 433
Model organism OurBigBook.com
Can a gene from Schizosaccharomyces pombe replace a missing function in Saccharomyces cerevisiae? A modern laboratory project tested functional complementation of methionine synthesis. For each tested gene deletion, the investigators compared plasmids carrying the corresponding Saccharomyces cerevisiae gene, a candidate Schizosaccharomyces pombe gene, and an unrelated gene. The first was a positive scientific control; the last was a negative scientific control. The paper describes this design rather than publishing a complete set of individual growth measurements. [ref]
The recipient biological strains also lacked the ability to make uracil. The pYES2.1/V5-His plasmids carried URA3, a gene restoring that ability, and used the GAL1 gene promoter to control the inserted gene. Initial plates lacked uracil but supplied methionine: this selected biological colonies containing plasmids without requiring successful methionine synthesis. Subsequent plates lacking methionine tested the missing function, comparing galactose induction with glucose conditions. Thus selecting for a plasmid and testing its functional contribution were separate operations. [ref]
The apparatus can be simple and informative. In the associated protocol, replica plating uses a block covered with velveteen to transfer small samples of biological colonies from a master plate onto plates with different nutrient conditions. Orientation marks preserve correspondence between locations; gentle contact limits the transferred material. The specified replicas omit uracil and methionine with either inducing sugar or glucose, and include a fresh glucose plate supplying methionine. The readout is growth at corresponding locations, not a direct measurement of enzyme activity. [ref]
The scientific controls answer different objections. Growth on the methionine-supplied replica checks survival and transfer. Rescue by the native gene checks that this biological strain and assay can reveal functional complementation. The unrelated gene tests whether carrying a plasmid alone is sufficient. Comparing induction conditions checks dependence on gene expression, although changing the sugar also changes metabolism: it is not an isolated change of gene expression in every other respect.
If the candidate gene restores growth while those comparisons behave as intended, it supplies a function sufficient for the tested growth requirement in this recipient. Failure to rescue is less decisive: the candidate protein might not be produced, might be altered by its attached tag, or might not work in this cellular context. The investigators therefore also used Western blots to examine protein production. A detected protein still does not establish correct protein folding or catalytic activity. [ref]

Model organism evidence transfer

Words: 206
Model organism OurBigBook.com
Evidence transfers at a stated level. Sequence alignment can suggest a candidate relationship between genes; functional complementation tests whether a candidate can supply a particular function in a chosen recipient. Neither alone establishes identical native gene expression, identical signal transduction, or identical consequences in every species. The yeast cross-species complementation experiment is especially useful because it tests a conserved function by intervention rather than assuming it from resemblance. [ref]
Even successful functional complementation occurs within a specific genetic background, nutrient supply and imposed gene expression. The enzyme may work with the recipient’s available substrates and partner proteins at an experimentally imposed abundance. Establishing the same role in the donor species calls for experiments there; establishing behavior under another condition calls for experiments under that condition. A conserved component can therefore coexist with context-dependent behavior of an entire pathway. This separation makes model organisms powerful: an accessible experiment supplies a precise mechanistic foothold and a better question for the next system.

Taxonomy (biology)

Words: 1k Articles: 10
Biology OurBigBook.com
Taxonomy names and classifies organisms. Classification can organize known diversity and make comparisons useful, but ranks and names are not themselves evidence of ancestry. Phylogenetics infers that ancestry; a clade includes an ancestor and all its descendants. A shared feature such as lacking a cell nucleus need not identify an exclusive clade. The organism branch here organizes cell types for reading and is not a proposed phylogenetic tree. See OpenStax Biology 2e, 20.1: classification and evolutionary history.

Domain (biology)

Words: 247 Articles: 2
Taxonomy (biology) OurBigBook.com
A biological domain is a high-level rank used to classify organisms in the three-domain system. Distinguish a taxonomic rank from a primary branch in an inferred phylogenetic tree: retaining familiar names does not settle the branching relationships.

Three-domain system

Words: 87
Domain (biology) OurBigBook.com
The three-domain system recognizes bacteria, archaea and eukaryotes as three domains. In 1990, Woese, Kandler and Wheelis proposed the domain rank and the names Bacteria, Archaea and Eucarya, using molecular comparisons to argue that the older prokaryote/eukaryote division hid important differences. See Woese, Kandler and Wheelis, 1990: Towards a natural system of organisms.
The associated three-domain ancestry model places the nuclear lineage of eukaryotes alongside archaea, rather than within them. This historically influential interpretation should be distinguished from the two-domain system; listing three familiar groups does not establish three independent primary branches.

Two-domain system

Words: 127
Domain (biology) OurBigBook.com
The two-domain system recognizes bacteria and archaea as the two primary lineages, placing the nuclear ancestry of eukaryotes within archaea. In this model, archaea as a complete clade includes that eukaryotic lineage; restricting the name to prokaryotic members describes a different grouping. Williams and colleagues' study, published online in 2019 and in a 2020 journal issue, found support for this model and a close relationship to Asgard archaea. See Williams et al., 2020: Phylogenomics provides robust support for a two-domains tree of life.
This updates the interpretation of the 1977 and 1990 classifications rather than undoing their discovery of deep differences between bacteria and archaea. Deep phylogenetic trees depend on the sampled genes, organisms and inference model; the precise closest archaeal relatives and early sequence of events require further evidence. Bacterial ancestry of mitochondria through endosymbiosis is a separate part of eukaryotic history.

Species

Words: 778 Articles: 6
Taxonomy (biology) OurBigBook.com
A species is a named unit of biological classification. The useful criteria vary among groups: reproductive compatibility can inform classification in many animals, while microbial comparisons also use genomes and other characters. Escherichia coli is a species; K-12 MG1655 identifies a particular strain within it. See OpenStax Biology 2e, 18.2: species concepts.

Species concept

Words: 397 Articles: 3
Species OurBigBook.com
A species concept states what should make organisms members of the same species; an operational criterion states what observations will test that claim. Reproductive isolation, distinguishable morphology and ancestry inferred through phylogenetics answer different questions. In a lineage-based interpretation, they are evidence for separation of evolving biological populations, and need not appear together. [ref]
Biological species concept
Words: 117
Species concept OurBigBook.com
The biological species concept groups naturally interbreeding biological populations with viable, fertile offspring, distinguished from other such groups by reproductive isolation. An operational test examines mating, fertilization, offspring survival and offspring reproduction, rather than only whether two adults can be paired. Sexual reproduction is its scope: fossils and organisms studied only through asexual reproduction cannot supply the same mating evidence. [ref]
For an original hypothetical example, imagine two separated biological populations that reproduce successfully after contact. The separation alone did not demonstrate reproductive isolation. Conversely, failure to mate in one unfamiliar chamber could reflect the assay conditions. Field observations of gene flow and tests under suitable conditions address the biological question more directly. A successful laboratory pairing does not establish frequent interbreeding in nature.
Morphological species concept
Words: 121
Species concept OurBigBook.com
A morphological species concept distinguishes species using morphology: measurable differences in form or structure. It can be applied to preserved specimens and fossils when mating cannot be observed. Similar appearance need not imply the same species, and different appearance need not imply different species. [ref]
An original operational example is to compare a chosen structure in specimens of comparable age, sex and rearing conditions. Suppose two apparent groups differ in size, but one group contains only juveniles. The observed difference does not yet diagnose two species. Specify the measured phenotype, variation within each sample, and whether the distinction persists across comparable specimens. A single striking specimen is a poor substitute for that comparison.
Phylogenetic species concept
Words: 97
Species concept OurBigBook.com
Phylogenetic species concepts use ancestry and diagnostic inherited differences; versions differ over requiring a clade, an exclusive ancestry pattern at genetic loci, or a distinguishable character combination. State which criterion is intended. [ref]
For an original operational example, suppose a phylogenetic tree inferred from one genetic locus separates two sampled biological populations. Compare further genetic loci and additional local samples before interpreting that branch as a species boundary. Otherwise the test may merely identify the particular ancestry of the sampled alleles. Adding more sites from the same genetic locus improves that locus's evidence without creating an independent ancestry test.

Species delimitation

Words: 233
Species OurBigBook.com
Species delimitation infers the boundaries and number of species from evidence. No single arbitrary percentage of nucleotide sequence difference is a universal boundary. Divergence within an old, widespread species can exceed divergence between recently separated species; geography and multiple kinds of evidence matter. [ref]
An original counterexample to a universal percentage rule: an assay could examine a strongly conserved gene in one comparison and a rapidly changing nucleotide sequence in another. Equal percentages then answer different historical questions. Even the denominator needs specifying: all sites, aligned sites, or only a filtered region? A threshold is an operational rule for a stated assay and group of organisms, whose errors need evaluating. It is not a definition that automatically transfers to every species.
The diagram's hypothetical pair B has similar morphology but reduced mating and distinct ancestry evidence. A morphological species concept could miss that distinction. Pair C instead has different morphology but compatible mating and ancestry that fails to separate the samples. That combination calls for checking variation in phenotype within a species. Pair A has only a structural difference observed: the other criteria remain untested. These examples show why missing evidence, disagreeing evidence and agreeing evidence require different interpretations.

Species, populations and strains

Words: 99
Species OurBigBook.com
A species can encompass many biological populations. A biological population specifies a set of organisms in a place and time; a biological strain identifies a maintained variant or lineage, often in a laboratory. A species name, a local census and a biological strain designation therefore describe different things. Multiple independently maintained cultures can also share the same biological strain designation.
For example, a culture identified as Escherichia coli K-12 MG1655 specifies more than the species alone. Two flasks inoculated from that culture are separate experimental biological populations; the separate containers do not establish two species or two different biological strains. This is an original experimental bookkeeping example, not a claim that every biological strain name encodes a complete genotype.

Heart development OurBigBook.com
myocardium acquiring chamber-associated growth, structural and electrophysiological properties, distinct from specialized non-chamber territories.

Cardiac looping

Words: 18
Heart development OurBigBook.com
Three-dimensional bending and torsion of the early heart tube. Geometry, left–right patterning, tissue growth and regional cell differentiation contribute distinct aspects.

Heart tube

Words: 53 Articles: 2
Heart development OurBigBook.com
An early tubular cardiac structure whose construction includes tissue convergence, differentiation and continued addition of cells at its poles.
Venous pole of the heart
Words: 20
Heart tube OurBigBook.com
The inflow end of the developing heart, with progenitors contributing to inflow and atrial regions under species- and stage-specific conditions.
Arterial pole of the heart
Words: 14
Heart tube OurBigBook.com
The outflow end of the developing heart, receiving progenitor contributions on a stage-specific schedule.

Cardiac crescent

Words: 15
Heart development OurBigBook.com
An early arrangement of cardiogenic tissue before formation of the linear heart tube in the mammalian embryo.

First heart field

Words: 31
Heart development OurBigBook.com
An early cardiac progenitor domain that differentiates into much of the initial myocardium, with major contributions to the left ventricle in mouse. Its boundaries and contributions require stage- and species-specific fate mapping.

Homeotic transformation

Words: 25
Developmental biology OurBigBook.com
Replacement of one position-specific developmental identity by another. Demonstrating it requires positive evidence for the alternative identity as well as loss of the original features.

Developmental timing

Words: 22
Developmental biology OurBigBook.com
The timing and ordering of specification, differentiation, tissue movement and maturation. Equal chronological age need not imply equal developmental stage after perturbation.

Lung development

Words: 62 Articles: 4
Developmental biology OurBigBook.com

Fetal breathing movement

Words: 22
Lung development OurBigBook.com
Movement before air breathing that contributes to fluid-related mechanical stimulation of the developing lung. Physical loading and mature respiratory function are distinct.

Alveolar epithelium

Words: 40 Articles: 2
Lung development OurBigBook.com
The epithelial lining of pulmonary gas-exchange units, containing differently specialized cell types.
Type II alveolar cell
Words: 12
Alveolar epithelium OurBigBook.com
An alveolar epithelial cell with secretory functions including surfactant production and context-dependent progenitor activity.
Type I alveolar cell
Words: 16
Alveolar epithelium OurBigBook.com
A thin, extended epithelial cell contributing to the gas-exchange surface. Flattening and molecular differentiation should be measured separately.

Skin development

Words: 22 Articles: 1
Developmental biology OurBigBook.com

Feather placode

Words: 22
Skin development OurBigBook.com
A localized epithelial primordium of a feather. Its molecular identity and underlying dermal aggregation can be coupled through mechanical and chemical signals.

Developmental competence

Words: 29
Developmental biology OurBigBook.com
The ability of a cell or tissue to respond to an instructive signal at a particular stage and location. The same signal can have different effects after competence changes.

Neural development

Words: 91 Articles: 4
Developmental biology OurBigBook.com
Formation and organization of nervous-system cells and their connections.

Neural progenitor cell

Words: 50 Articles: 1
Neural development OurBigBook.com
A precursor able to produce one or more neural cell types. multipotency is a property of an individual progenitor under tested conditions, not merely of a mixed population.
Radial glial cell
Words: 24
Neural progenitor cell OurBigBook.com
A neural progenitor with radial processes and context-dependent neuronal or glial outputs. cell morphology, molecular state and traced descendants provide complementary evidence for its role.

Neuronal differentiation

Words: 23
Neural development OurBigBook.com
Acquisition of neuronal identity and function. Commitment, subtype specification, maturation and survival should be measured separately rather than inferred from one neuronal marker.

Axon guidance

Words: 9
Neural development OurBigBook.com
Processes directing growing axons to appropriate regions or targets.

Epicardium

Words: 20
Developmental biology OurBigBook.com
The outer tissue layer covering the heart, with developmental contributions to supporting cells and signals affecting myocardial and coronary development.

Endocardium

Words: 15
Developmental biology OurBigBook.com
The inner endothelial lining of the heart, which also provides developmental signals to neighbouring myocardium.

Second heart field

Words: 26
Developmental biology OurBigBook.com
A population of cardiac progenitors that contributes cells to the developing heart after initial heart-tube formation. Retaining a proliferative reservoir allows progressive addition of differentiated myocardium.

Regeneration

Words: 46 Articles: 1
Developmental biology OurBigBook.com
Replacement of lost biological structures through organized growth and differentiation. Recovery of mass alone need not demonstrate restoration of the original pattern or function.

Blastema

Words: 22
Regeneration OurBigBook.com
A regeneration-associated accumulation of progenitor cells. A blastema need not be a homogeneous pluripotent population; contributors can retain tissue and positional restrictions.

Positional information

Words: 55 Articles: 1
Developmental biology OurBigBook.com
Information allowing a cell to respond according to its location within a developing or regenerating structure. Establishing a positional value and interpreting it as a differentiated outcome are distinct steps.

Positional memory

Words: 25
Positional information OurBigBook.com
Persistence of a position-associated cellular identity after the original spatial context or instructive signal changes. It is distinct from simply retaining a differentiated tissue identity.

Intestinal development

Words: 38 Articles: 1
Developmental biology OurBigBook.com
Formation, regionalization and maturation of the intestine, including its epithelial surface, supporting tissues and renewing cell populations.

Villus morphogenesis

Words: 21
Intestinal development OurBigBook.com
Formation of epithelial villi through interactions among growth, tissue constraints and local signalling. The ordering of these events differs between species.

Mesenchyme

Words: 24
Developmental biology OurBigBook.com
A tissue organization with cells dispersed through extracellular matrix, rather than arranged as a continuous polarized epithelium. Mesenchymal populations differ in origin and developmental potential.

Fate mapping

Words: 28
Developmental biology OurBigBook.com
Assignment of later cellular or tissue contributions to identified precursor regions. Labels require positional and persistence controls; observed fate alone is not a complete test of evolutionary identity.

Limb bud

Words: 143 Articles: 6
Developmental biology OurBigBook.com
An embryonic appendage precursor whose growth, signalling and cellular contributions can be compared between forelimbs and hindlimbs.

Autopod

Words: 11
Limb bud OurBigBook.com
The distal limb region including wrist or ankle elements and digits.

Zeugopod

Words: 17
Limb bud OurBigBook.com
The intermediate limb region containing the radius and ulna, or tibia and fibula, in familiar tetrapod limbs.

Stylopod

Words: 13
Limb bud OurBigBook.com
The proximal limb region containing the humerus or femur in familiar tetrapod limbs.

Progress zone

Words: 32
Limb bud OurBigBook.com
A classical model in which time spent in a distal region of the growing limb contributes to proximal-distal specification. Experimental support must be distinguished from alternative consequences of altered survival and growth.

Apical ectodermal ridge

Words: 29
Limb bud OurBigBook.com
A specialized distal ectodermal structure that supplies signals supporting limb outgrowth and patterning. Removing it simultaneously alters several processes, so truncation alone does not uniquely identify a timing mechanism.

Zone of polarizing activity

Words: 25
Limb bud OurBigBook.com
A posterior limb-bud signalling region involved in anterior–posterior patterning. The fate of its labelled cells and the identities of adjacent anatomical digits are related but distinct observations.

ABC model of flower development

Words: 41
Developmental biology OurBigBook.com
A model relating overlapping regulatory functions to floral organ identities. B- and C-function activity contributes to male organ identity, whereas C activity without B contributes to female identity, with additional partners required. Its simple domains are not universal across all angiosperms.

Developmental modularity

Words: 24
Developmental biology OurBigBook.com
Organization of biological development into relatively separable components. It can allow one structure or deployment to evolve with fewer effects on others, without implying complete independence.

Developmental bias

Words: 29
Developmental biology OurBigBook.com
Unequal accessibility of phenotypic variants caused by the organization of biological development. Repeated outcomes can reflect this structure as well as repeated natural selection; accessibility and selective advantage are different questions.

Serial homology

Words: 22
Developmental biology OurBigBook.com
Correspondence among repeated structures within an organism, such as repeated appendages or segments. Repeated structures can subsequently specialize through divergent developmental regulation.

Heterotopy

Words: 23
Developmental biology OurBigBook.com
An evolutionary change in the spatial deployment of a developmental process. Altering where a regulatory input is expressed can change the resulting pattern.

Deep homology

Words: 28
Developmental biology OurBigBook.com
Shared inherited developmental machinery underlying structures whose final organization can differ substantially. A shared regulator alone does not establish that two entire organs have the same historical origin.

Gene co-option

Words: 25
Developmental biology OurBigBook.com
Recruitment of an existing gene or gene regulatory network to a new developmental deployment or function. Changing the location of gene expression can generate a new structure using inherited cellular activities.

Evolutionary developmental biology

Words: 170 Articles: 4
Developmental biology OurBigBook.com
Study of how changes in biological development contribute to evolution. Comparative gene expression, developmental perturbations and phylogenetics can connect inherited mechanisms to new forms.

Heterometry

Words: 26
Evolutionary developmental biology OurBigBook.com
Evolutionary change in the amount or level of a developmental process, structure or expression pattern. A quantitative difference still requires a causal molecular and developmental explanation.

Digit identity frameshift hypothesis (CII​,CIII​,CIV​↦DI​,DII​,DIII​)

Words: 42
Evolutionary developmental biology OurBigBook.com
The classical avian hypothesis that anatomical digit identities I, II and III are expressed at positional condensations II, III and IV. It distinguishes position from developmental identity; evidence for a limited anterior shift does not require invariant identities for every posterior anatomical digit.[ref]

Mostly male theory

Words: 37
Evolutionary developmental biology OurBigBook.com
A specific historical hypothesis in which ectopic ovules arose on a predominantly male precursor during flower evolution. It combines gene-history and morphological arguments but remains distinct from a demonstrated ancestral developmental sequence.[ref]

Out-of-male hypothesis

Words: 45
Evolutionary developmental biology OurBigBook.com
A proposed origin of a bisexual reproductive structure through regional modification of a formerly male structure. In one developmental scenario, restriction of B-class activity permits female identity in part of a C-active reproductive axis. Accessibility in a model system does not establish the historical precursor.

New Head hypothesis

Words: 31
Developmental biology OurBigBook.com
The hypothesis that integration of neural crest, ectodermal placodes and other cranial tissues helped enable vertebrate head innovation and more active feeding. Developmental necessity, morphological diversification and ancestral ecological reconstruction are different evidential claims.

Germ layer

Words: 59 Articles: 2
Developmental biology OurBigBook.com
A principal embryonic cellular layer established through gastrulation; the classical three-layer organisation comprises ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm.

Mesendoderm

Words: 43 Articles: 1
Germ layer OurBigBook.com
A developmental designation for mesodermal and endodermal progenitors or a shared regulatory state. A shared marker profile does not prove every individual cell is bipotent.
Prechordal plate
Words: 19
Mesendoderm OurBigBook.com
An anterior axial mesendodermal population with morphogenetic and signalling roles. In zebrafish its coherent migration depends on contact-mediated directional information.

Endoderm

Words: 81 Articles: 2
Developmental biology OurBigBook.com
An embryonic germ layer contributing to the epithelial lining of much of the digestive and respiratory systems and associated organs.

Definitive endoderm

Words: 21
Endoderm OurBigBook.com
The embryonic endoderm population specified during gastrulation, distinguished from earlier extraembryonic primitive endoderm. In mouse, resulting gut endoderm can include intercalated cells from distinct histories.

Endoderm specification in Caenorhabditis elegans

Words: 42
Endoderm OurBigBook.com
The E blastomere produces the intestinal lineage. Maternal SKN-1 and the P2-to-EMS inductive interaction converge on an endoderm gene regulatory network with parallel inputs and partly redundant GATA transcription factors. Loss of one late marker does not establish loss of the lineage.[ref]

Pharyngeal arch

Words: 44 Articles: 2
Developmental biology OurBigBook.com
A repeated embryonic pharyngeal structure assembled from several tissues, including neural crest, mesoderm, ectoderm and endoderm.

Branchial arch

Words: 30 Articles: 1
Pharyngeal arch OurBigBook.com
A gill-bearing pharyngeal arch and its associated tissues.
Branchial ray
Words: 24
Branchial arch OurBigBook.com
A cartilaginous projection supporting the gill apparatus in living cartilaginous fishes. It is not the same structure as a bony-fish gill raker or a dermal fin ray.

Ectodermal placode

Words: 21
Developmental biology OurBigBook.com
A localised ectodermal thickening or precursor territory contributing to cranial sensory structures and associated cells. Placodes and neural crest make distinct interacting contributions.

Mesoderm

Words: 34 Articles: 1
Developmental biology OurBigBook.com
An embryonic germ layer supplying diverse tissues, including muscle and much connective tissue; particular connective tissues can also arise from ectoderm-derived neural crest.

Lateral plate mesoderm

Words: 14
Mesoderm OurBigBook.com
Lateral embryonic mesoderm contributing to body-wall, visceral and paired-appendage tissues under species- and stage-specific arrangements.

Ectoderm

Words: 15
Developmental biology OurBigBook.com
An embryonic germ layer giving rise to epidermal and neural tissues, including the origin of vertebrate neural crest.

Neural crest

Words: 39
Developmental biology OurBigBook.com
A vertebrate embryonic population arising near the neural border, with migratory descendants contributing to cranial connective and skeletal tissues, peripheral neurons and glia, pigment cells and other derivatives. Individual cells and axial populations have restricted subsets of these potentials.

Cellularization

Words: 13
Developmental biology OurBigBook.com
Formation of individual cell boundaries around nuclei previously sharing a common cytoplasmic compartment.

Syncytial specification

Words: 40 Articles: 1
Developmental biology OurBigBook.com
Positional specification of nuclei in a shared cytoplasm before complete cellularization, allowing spatial signals to influence nuclear transcription without conventional cell boundaries.

Syncytial blastoderm

Words: 19
Syncytial specification OurBigBook.com
An early insect embryonic stage with many nuclei sharing cytoplasm before cellularization. Transcriptional patterning can therefore precede formation of individual cell boundaries.

Mosaic development

Words: 27
Developmental biology OurBigBook.com
A pattern of development with relatively restricted adjustment after early cell loss or isolation. A missing structure after injury alone does not establish an irreversibly preassigned fate.

Regulative development

Words: 29
Developmental biology OurBigBook.com
Development in which cells can adjust their contributions after perturbation, for example replacing an ablated lineage. Tracing the source of replacement distinguishes fate conversion from expansion of residual cells.

Heterochrony

Words: 23
Developmental biology OurBigBook.com
An evolutionary change in the timing or relative rates of developmental processes. It can alter outcomes without requiring a wholly new developmental mechanism.

Segment addition zone

Words: 22
Developmental biology OurBigBook.com
A posterior embryonic region associated with sequential production of body segments; local timing and cell displacement convert changing programmes into spatial order.

Clock and wavefront model

Words: 32
Developmental biology OurBigBook.com
A model in which a temporal oscillator is converted into repeated spatial boundaries as tissue passes a maturation front. With steady relative front speed v and period T, predicted spacing is vT.

Presomitic mesoderm

Words: 6
Developmental biology OurBigBook.com
Unsegmented posterior paraxial mesoderm from which somites are generated.

Amnion

Words: 18
Developmental biology OurBigBook.com
An extraembryonic membrane associated with the amniotic cavity; its early formation and geometry differ among mammalian developmental systems.

Hypoblast

Words: 61 Articles: 2
Developmental biology OurBigBook.com
An early mammalian lineage contributing to extraembryonic endodermal tissues. It is distinct from the definitive endoderm produced during gastrulation.

Visceral endoderm

Words: 43 Articles: 1
Hypoblast OurBigBook.com
An extraembryonic endodermal epithelium associated with early mammalian development. It supplies signals and matrix and must be distinguished from definitive endoderm formed through gastrulation.
Anterior visceral endoderm
Words: 22
Visceral endoderm OurBigBook.com
A signalling region that becomes positioned on the prospective anterior side of the mouse embryo and antagonizes posteriorizing signals, helping position the primitive streak.

Inner cell mass

Words: 12
Developmental biology OurBigBook.com
The internal cell population of a mammalian blastocyst that separates into epiblast and hypoblast.

Trophectoderm

Words: 40 Articles: 1
Developmental biology OurBigBook.com
The outer lineage of a mammalian blastocyst, contributing to extraembryonic trophoblast tissues rather than the embryo proper.

Extraembryonic ectoderm

Words: 23
Trophectoderm OurBigBook.com
A trophoblast-derived tissue adjacent to the early mouse epiblast. Its signalling interactions help organize gastrulation, while it is not itself an epiblast-derived germ layer.

Somitogenesis

Words: 13
Developmental biology OurBigBook.com
The formation of somites from presomitic mesoderm, coordinated with posterior tissue supply and the segmentation clock.

Somite

Words: 20
Developmental biology OurBigBook.com
One of the serial paired embryonic units produced from presomitic mesoderm; its derivatives contribute to axial skeletal, muscular and dermal tissues.

Neural tube

Words: 16
Developmental biology OurBigBook.com
An embryonic epithelial structure giving rise to the central nervous system, including the brain and spinal cord in vertebrates.

Notochord

Words: 12
Developmental biology OurBigBook.com
An axial tissue of chordates that provides structural and signalling functions during development.

A tissue narrows in one direction and lengthens in another through coordinated cell movements, often involving cell intercalation. Elongation need not imply increased tissue volume.

The mesoderm flanking the axial midline that produces somites during somitogenesis.

A posterior embryonic region that supplies cells to the extending body axis; its contribution to tissue growth and rearrangement varies with species and stage.

The transient region through which cells ingress during amniote gastrulation, supplying mesoderm and definitive endoderm.

The coordinated rearrangements that establish the principal germ layers and their relative positions in an early embryo.

Elongation of the early fly embryonic tissue through processes including polarized junction remodelling and cell intercalation. Neighbour changes and individual cell-shape changes make separable contributions to tissue deformation.

Formation of projecting myocardial structures on the luminal side of a ventricular wall. Differentiation, adhesion, rearrangement and proliferation can contribute, so absent trabeculae do not uniquely diagnose a division defect.

Creation and organization of an internal space in a tissue. Polarized surface delivery, division orientation, fluid transport and sometimes cell clearance can contribute; a cavity alone does not identify its mechanism.

An epithelial enclosure around a lumen, used experimentally to study coordinated polarity, division and surface traffic. Multiple lumina do not necessarily imply loss of polarity in every cell.

Alteration of cellular geometry, which can contribute to tissue deformation without a change in cell number. Its contribution can be distinguished from neighbour exchange by following cell outlines over time.

Paleontology OurBigBook.com
Study of processes between an organism's death and observation of its remains, including transport, decay, burial and preservation. These processes bias the fossil and archaeological record.

Processes through which biological remains or traces enter the fossil record. Complete replacement by new minerals is only one possible pathway.

Preservation retaining anatomical information normally removed by decay or burial alteration. It reflects particular preservational pathways, not an unbiased sample of all life.

Reworking of fossils

Taphonomy OurBigBook.com
Erosion and redeposition of previously buried remains into a younger deposit, potentially confusing environmental and chronological interpretation.

Taphonomic transport

Taphonomy OurBigBook.com
Movement of remains by currents, waves, gravity or organisms. Sorting depends on size, density, shape and articulation rather than solely on taxon abundance.
Hydraulic sorting
Words: 18
Taphonomic transport OurBigBook.com
Differential movement or deposition of remains by flowing water, dependent on their shape, density, size, orientation and articulation.

Disarticulation

Taphonomy OurBigBook.com
Separation of connected skeletal elements as supporting tissues fail or external forces act. An articulated skeleton need not have been buried instantly.

Taphonomy OurBigBook.com
Transformation and loss of biological tissues after death through autolysis, microbial activity and associated processes. Decay rates differ among anatomical characters.
Autolysis

Enzymatic breakdown of cells by their own components after loss of normal regulation.

Biostratinomy

Processes affecting remains before final burial, including decay, disarticulation, transport and surface modification. These mechanisms can continue or recur during reworking.

Physical and chemical alteration after burial, potentially modifying fossil tissues and isotopic compositions.

Change in the crystal organization of fossil material during alteration, potentially obscuring original histological or chemical information.

precipitation or replacement by minerals during burial alteration. Early mineral formation can retain fine biological detail, while later alteration can destroy or obscure it.

Reduction of sediment volume during burial that can flatten, distort or fracture enclosed remains.

Preservation or replication by calcium phosphate minerals, sometimes retaining soft-tissue detail when precipitation occurs before its destruction.

Preservation retaining anatomical information normally lost, especially soft tissues. Such deposits reveal otherwise hidden diversity but still select particular environments and tissue types.

Erosion of an older deposit and incorporation of its fossil material into a younger one. It can create a misleading apparent last occurrence.

Movement before final burial can sort remains by size, shape and density. Articulation alone cannot prove local origin, and disarticulation alone cannot prove transport.

A collection of fossil remains associated in a specified deposit or sample. Its members may have different original habitats or ages; transport of fossil remains and time averaging affect its interpretation.

An assemblage containing remains transported from their original living sites. Hydraulic sorting can enrich durable parts or mix habitats; transport does not invariably disarticulate a carcass.

Words: 26

An assemblage whose organisms are preserved where they lived. Local origin does not eliminate taphonomic bias: soft tissues can disappear and resistant parts can accumulate through time.

Taphonomy OurBigBook.com
Systematic distortion of biological information through differential preservation and recovery. teeth and delicate soft tissues need not have the same probability of entering the fossil record; even a locally buried assemblage can therefore give a biased account of its living community.

Erroneous placement toward the base of a lineage when loss of diagnostic characters through carcass decay is interpreted as an ancestral biological absence. Coding unobservable characters as unknown and comparing preservation across specimens can reduce the problem.

Morphogen

Words: 1k Articles: 6
Biology OurBigBook.com
A morphogen is a signal whose spatial concentration helps specify different biological cell fates or behaviors during biological development. A morphogen gradient provides a positional cue: biological cells at different distances from a source experience different local concentrations and can follow different developmental pathways. A spatial concentration variation alone does not establish that a substance is a morphogen; its graded developmental effects matter. See Alberts et al., Molecular Biology of the Cell, 4th edition (2002): morphogens as graded developmental signals.
The beautiful idea is that one distributed signal can help organize several regions of a developing body. A continuous morphogen gradient can supply the input for distinct domains of gene expression, rather than requiring a separate signal for every position. A morphogen response threshold is a useful idealization of that interpretation: high, intermediate and low concentrations are assigned different outcomes. The morphogen reaction-diffusion equation describes one way to generate a morphogen gradient; the equation is a model of transport and reaction, while the morphogen is the signal being transported.
Detection and interpretation also depend on the receiving biological cell. For an extracellular morphogen, receptors and signal transduction connect the local concentration to a response; receptor binding occupancy is only one step in that connection. The same morphogen gradient can be interpreted differently in different tissues because their developmental context differs. Thus a morphogen response threshold summarizes a particular response in a particular context, rather than being a universal property of the signal. See Scott F. Gilbert, Developmental Biology, 6th edition (2000): positional information and context-dependent interpretation.
An important experimental example came in 1988. Wolfgang Driever and Christiane Nüsslein-Volhard used antibodies to examine the bicoid protein in early fruit-fly embryos. They reported a concentration profile approximately described by an exponential function, highest at the front, with the protein concentrated in cell nuclei. Their abstract proposed diffusion from localized messenger RNA and dispersed degradation as a likely origin of the morphogen gradient, rather than proving a unique transport mechanism. [ref]
In a companion study, Driever and Nüsslein-Volhard genetically changed the amount and distribution of bicoid messenger RNA, measured the resulting protein morphogen gradient, and compared developmental maps. Increased local bicoid protein levels shifted prospective anterior structures toward the rear; decreased levels shifted them toward the front. This linked a measured concentration profile to positional effects in biological development. The toy calculations below illustrate that logic with arbitrary numbers, not measured bicoid parameters. [ref]
