Morphogen gradient (c(x))

Words: 357 Articles: 1
Morphogen OurBigBook.com
A morphogen gradient is a spatially varying concentration profile of a morphogen. The profile c(x) specifies the local amount; its mathematical gradient, c′(x) in one dimension, specifies how rapidly that amount changes with position. In the simplest positional interpretation, a biological cell responds to its local concentration, without having to measure the gradient across itself. Production, transport and removal together determine a morphogen gradient.
For a worked example, take a stationary one-dimensional tissue occupying x≥0, constant diffusion coefficient D>0, and uniform first-order reaction removal at rate k>0. At steady state, this specialization of the morphogen reaction-diffusion equation gives the ordinary differential equation and boundary conditions
Ddx2d2c​−kc=0,c(0)=c0​,limx→∞​c(x)=0.
(16)
Here D has units of length squared per time, k has units of inverse time, and c0​ is a prescribed source concentration. The Dirichlet boundary condition fixes the concentration at x=0. It does not prescribe a source flux; any required flux follows from the solution. These assumptions define a toy morphogen gradient, not a universal account of transport during biological development.
Define the diffusion length ℓ=D/k​. Substitution into the ordinary differential equation shows that its general solution is Aex/ℓ+Be−x/ℓ. The vanishing boundary condition at infinity forces A=0, and the source Dirichlet boundary condition forces B=c0​. Hence
c(x)=c0​e−x/ℓ,ℓ=D/k​.
(17)
Over every additional diffusion length, the concentration falls by the same factor e−1. Faster diffusion increases ℓ; faster removal decreases ℓ. This makes the diffusion length a useful bridge between microscopic transport and the spatial reach of a morphogen gradient.
Choose c0​=100 arbitrary concentration units and ℓ=100μm, where 1μm=10−6m. Then c(x)=100e−x/(100μm): at x=0, 100μm and 200μm, the concentrations are 100, approximately 36.79 and approximately 13.53. The following diagram combines this morphogen gradient with the idealized responses calculated under morphogen response threshold.

Morphogen source-diffusion-degradation model (λ=D/k​)

Words: 35
Morphogen gradient OurBigBook.com
An idealized model balancing localized production, diffusion and degradation. In one dimension at steady state, away from the source, Dc′′−kc=0 gives c(x)=c0​e−x/λ with λ=D/k​. Tissue geometry and time-dependent source distributions can invalidate a simple point-source interpretation.

Morphogen response threshold (θ)

Words: 457
Morphogen OurBigBook.com
A morphogen response threshold is a concentration level used to distinguish developmental responses to a morphogen. In an idealized threshold model, otherwise equivalent biological cells exposed to c≥θ take one response and those exposed to c<θ take another. Two morphogen response thresholds can assign three bands: fate A for c≥50, fate B for 20≤c<50, and fate C for c<20, all in the toy arbitrary concentration units. The A/B/C labels specify a response rule, not named cell types or a claim that every morphogen produces sharp boundaries. See the positional-information model in Gilbert's reference under morphogen.
For the decreasing morphogen gradient c(x)=c0​e−x/ℓ and 0<θ<c0​, solve c(xθ​)=θ using the natural logarithm:
xθ​=ℓln(θc0​​).
(18)
With c0​=100 and diffusion length ℓ=100μm, the morphogen response thresholds 50 and 20 give
x50​=100ln2μm≈69.3147μm,x20​=100ln5μm≈160.9438μm.
(19)
Thus fate A occupies 0≤x≤x50​, fate B occupies x50​<x≤x20​, and fate C occupies x>x20​ in this idealization. The equality convention belongs to the response rule. If θ=c0​, the crossing is at the source; if θ>c0​, that morphogen response threshold is never reached anywhere in the tissue.
Now double the prescribed source concentration from c0​ to 2c0​, keeping D, k, diffusion length ℓ and a fixed morphogen response threshold 0<θ<c0​ unchanged. The whole morphogen gradient doubles, but the boundary moves by an additive distance:
Δxθ​=ℓln(θ2c0​​)−ℓln(θc0​​)=ℓln2.
(20)
For θ=20, the crossing moves from 160.9438μm to 100ln10μm≈230.2585μm, a shift of 69.3147μm. Every fixed morphogen response threshold below the original source concentration shifts by this same distance in the toy model. The example compares two Dirichlet boundary conditions, c(0)=100 and c(0)=200; doubling an experimentally supplied source flux is a different boundary specification.
These calculations are useful because they separate changes in source concentration, diffusion length and response rule. Their limits are equally concrete: growing tissues change the geometry, a transient response can precede steady state, molecular fluctuations can blur a boundary, and signaling feedback or altered transport can change the morphogen gradient or its interpretation. A local instantaneous morphogen response threshold need not capture exposure duration, signaling adaptation or the receiving biological cell's state. Experiments on cultured human biological cells found different responses to the level and rate of change of developmental signals, illustrating why signal dynamics can matter. [ref] Quantitative measurements of bicoid protein and its downstream gene expression also make precision a question for experiment, rather than something guaranteed by drawing threshold lines. [ref] Morphogen gradients provide one mechanism for spatial patterning in biological development, alongside other signals and interactions.

Biology OurBigBook.com
Flow cytometry records signals from suspended particles passing an illuminated interrogation region. For a flow cytometric DNA-content assay, a laser excites a DNA-binding dye and a detector records its fluorescence. An event is a recorded passage, not a guarantee that exactly one intact biological cell was measured.

Flow cytometric DNA-content assay

Words: 300
Flow cytometry OurBigBook.com
Under controlled staining and detector settings, integrated fluorescence can be approximately proportional to nuclear DNA amount. A histogram of accepted single-cell events then separates a 2C region, an intermediate region and a 4C region. These are ordinarily assigned to G0 phase/G1 phase, S phase, and G2 phase/M phase respectively in the stated diploid model.
A Cornell protocol fixes a single-cell suspension by adding cold 70% ethanol dropwise while mixing, reducing clumping. After washing, its staining solution contains propidium iodide at 50μg/ml; ribonuclease A removes interfering RNA. It specifies excitation at 488nm and emission around 600nm. The resulting readout is fluorescence per event, not a direct count of chromosomes. [ref]
Useful controls include an unstained sample for background and a reference population with known nuclear DNA amount, processed with identical settings. Two attached 2C biological cells can mimic one 4C event. Comparing signal integral with pulse height or width helps exclude such doublets; a gate selecting intact single particles also limits debris. These are proposed assay checks, not measurements underlying the illustration.
A 4C peak cannot distinguish G2 phase from mitosis; a 2C peak cannot distinguish G1 phase from G0 phase. Mixed ploidy, uneven staining and aggregates can invalidate phase assignments. Peak areas describe the accepted sample at collection, and do not by themselves establish phase durations, division rates or a particular arrest mechanism. A treatment comparison needs matched handling and another readout appropriate to the claimed mechanism.

Metabolism

Words: 3k Articles: 67
Biology OurBigBook.com
The network of chemical reactions that maintains a living system, supplies energy and builds or processes its material. Gas emissions can arise as primary metabolic byproducts or secondary metabolic byproducts, with different implications for an atmospheric biosignature gas.
Enzymes make this network operate on biologically useful timescales. Following material through successive substrates and reaction products explains why a single fast enzyme need not make the entire network fast: another step may constrain the flow. Changing enzyme amounts or activity therefore changes which routes can carry material, connecting molecular chemical kinetics to the maintenance and growth of a biological cell. See Alberts et al., Molecular Biology of the Cell: multienzyme complexes and cell metabolism.

Photosynthesis

Words: 971 Articles: 27
Metabolism OurBigBook.com
Photosynthesis captures light energy and transforms it into chemical forms that a biological cell can use. In plants, algae and cyanobacteria, this supports carbon fixation: incorporation of carbon from carbon dioxide into chemical compounds used to build living material. Capturing light and incorporating carbon are distinct processes coupled through metabolism. See OpenStax Biology 2e, 8.1: overview of photosynthesis.
For oxygenic photosynthesis, a simplified net equation writes a six-carbon sugar, glucose, as the representative product:
6CO2​+6H2​O+light⟶C6​H12​O6​+6O2​.
(21)
This is net stoichiometry, not a one-step mechanism. A worked bookkeeping check counts six carbon chemical atoms, twelve hydrogen chemical atoms, and eighteen oxygen chemical atoms on each side: the product side has six oxygen chemical atoms in the sugar and twelve in molecular oxygen. The light label supplies energy, not additional chemical atoms.
Crucially, the released molecular oxygen comes from water, not carbon dioxide. Cancelling water made and consumed in different steps hides this distinction in the net equation. The Calvin cycle supplies a net three-carbon triose phosphate, such as glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate, for subsequent sugar synthesis; it does not directly export glucose. See OpenStax Biology 2e, 8.2: light-dependent reactions and OpenStax Biology 2e, 8.3: using light energy to make organic molecules.
The useful achievement is connecting incoming light to both usable energy and new biological material. ATP is an immediate energy currency; NADPH supplies electrons for synthesis; carbon dioxide supplies the carbon incorporated into carbohydrates. These roles are complementary. Conservation of energy still holds: photosynthesis transforms energy, never creates it, and some absorbed energy is dissipated as heat. A plant also carries out cellular respiration, including in biological cells that perform photosynthesis. Gas exchange reflects both processes. Oxygenic photosynthesis remains central to interpreting terrestrial molecular oxygen as an atmospheric biosignature gas. See OpenStax Biology 2e, 8.3: photosynthesis and respiration.

Metabolism OurBigBook.com
Carbon fixation incorporates carbon from carbon dioxide into organic chemical compounds. It identifies a material transformation, rather than a particular source of energy: carbon fixation can be supported by photosynthesis or by other metabolism. The Calvin cycle is one pathway, not the definition of all carbon fixation.

Calvin cycle

Words: 126 Articles: 1
Carbon fixation OurBigBook.com
The Calvin cycle couples carbon fixation to use of ATP and NADPH. In a chloroplast it takes place in the chloroplast stroma. Its chemical reactions incorporate carbon dioxide, use NADPH-supplied electrons, and regenerate the molecules that accept further carbon dioxide.
In the standard Calvin cycle bookkeeping, three carbon dioxide molecules require nine ATP and six NADPH for one net three-carbon triose phosphate. A six-carbon sugar equivalent therefore corresponds to six carbon dioxide, eighteen ATP and twelve NADPH; subsequent sugar synthesis is separate. These are pathway requirements, not a universal measured photosynthesis yield. See OpenStax Biology 2e, 8.3: Calvin cycle bookkeeping.
Calling the Calvin cycle light-independent means its individual chemical reactions do not directly capture light; it does not mean the Calvin cycle runs only at night or independently of the supplies from light-dependent reactions.

Calvin cycle OurBigBook.com
Ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate carboxylase/oxygenase, the enzyme catalysing carbon-dioxide addition to ribulose bisphosphate in the Calvin cycle. Its competing oxygenase reaction links carbon assimilation to photorespiration.

Cellular respiration

Words: 1k Articles: 10
Metabolism OurBigBook.com
Cellular respiration transfers energy from chemical fuels into usable forms including ATP. Oxidation of the fuel is coupled to reduction of an electron acceptor; the energy transfer can support ATP synthesis. Plants carry out cellular respiration as well as photosynthesis. Their biological cells need usable energy in darkness too, and a seed can draw on stored fuel during germination.[ref][ref]
Follow three different accounts: carbon moving from fuel to products, electrons moving to an electron acceptor, and energy becoming available for cellular work. They are connected, but an oxygen uptake measurement alone does not identify the fuel or count the ATP made. The pea seed respirometry experiment makes this distinction visible with simple apparatus.

Heterotrophic respiration (Rh​)

Words: 22
Cellular respiration OurBigBook.com
Respiratory carbon loss by organisms using organic matter produced by others. It includes important decomposer fluxes and must be distinguished from autotrophic respiration.

Autotrophic respiration (Ra​)

Words: 11
Cellular respiration OurBigBook.com
Respiratory carbon loss by primary producers. Subtracting it from gross primary production gives net primary production.

Aerobic respiration

Words: 449 Articles: 1
Cellular respiration OurBigBook.com
Aerobic respiration uses molecular oxygen as the final electron acceptor. For complete oxidation of glucose, the net material balance is
C6​H12​O6​+6O2​⟶6CO2​+6H2​O.
(22)
This records the overall conversion of glucose, molecular oxygen, carbon dioxide and water; it is not one enzyme-catalyzed step, and it omits the separate ATP accounting. For an original stoichiometry check, each side contains six carbon, twelve hydrogen and eighteen oxygen chemical atoms. If exactly 1mmol of glucose undergoes this complete conversion, the equation requires 6mmol of molecular oxygen and yields 6mmol each of carbon dioxide and net water. This is an equation-based calculation, not an observed seed measurement.
The molecular oxygen is reduced to water, rather than being the source of the carbon dioxide's carbon. A formal redox electron balance, using acidic half-reaction notation, makes the roles explicit:
C6​H12​O6​+6H2​O6O2​+24H++24e−​⟶6CO2​+24H++24e−,⟶12H2​O.​
(23)
Adding and cancelling gives the net equation above. Both half-reactions conserve chemical atoms and electric charge. The 24 electrons balance a net transfer; they are carried through cellular intermediates, rather than released as a pool of free electrons. The final respiratory reduction can be written O2​+4H++4e−⟶2H2​O. These equations are bookkeeping, not a tracing experiment that assigns every product oxygen chemical atom to its original molecule.[ref]
Respiration and ATP coupling (ADP+Pi​⟶ATP)
Words: 269
Aerobic respiration OurBigBook.com
Glycolysis converts glucose into two pyruvate molecules, with a net two ATP and reduced NADH; it does not directly consume molecular oxygen. Pyruvate processing and the citric acid cycle, also called the TCA cycle, release carbon dioxide and supply reduced carriers. Thus releasing carbon dioxide and consuming molecular oxygen occur at different stages.[ref]
An electron transport chain reoxidizes carriers such as NADH. Coupling some of its redox steps to proton transport establishes an electrochemical gradient; ATP synthase can use that gradient to form ATP from adenosine diphosphate and inorganic phosphate. This is oxidative phosphorylation. A separate route, substrate-level phosphorylation, transfers a phosphate group from a reacting substrate to adenosine diphosphate. In typical eukaryotic biological cells, the respiratory chain occupies the inner membrane of a mitochondrion.[ref]
The useful achievement is controlled transfer: fuel oxidation can replenish an ATP supply that supports active transport and synthesis. ATP is a reusable chemical carrier, not newly created energy; ATP hydrolysis and the coupled cellular process have their own net free energy balance. Some fuel energy is dissipated as heat.[ref]
There is no universal yield of 36 or 38 ATP per glucose. Actual ATP recovery depends on carrier transfer routes, coupling and diversion of intermediates to other metabolism. In particular, an oxygen uptake rate cannot be converted into an ATP production rate by assuming one fixed multiplier.[ref]

Anaerobic respiration

Words: 84
Cellular respiration OurBigBook.com
Anaerobic respiration uses a respiratory electron transport chain with a final electron acceptor other than molecular oxygen. External acceptors can include sulfate, depending on the organism. “External” distinguishes a supplied terminal acceptor from the fuel-derived organic intermediates used in fermentation; it does not mean that the reduction must take place outside the biological cell. In fermentation, regeneration of carriers such as NADH to their oxidized form permits glycolysis to continue without a respiratory electron transport chain. Both routes can operate without molecular oxygen, but they are different mechanisms.[ref]

Words: 633 Articles: 4
Cellular respiration OurBigBook.com
A respirometer measures gas changes associated with cellular respiration. In the absorber-based pea seed respirometry apparatus, the changing gas inventory is inferred from a liquid boundary's displacement. A respirometer is therefore a physical measurement coupled to a biological process, not a direct ATP counter.
Respirometry
Respirometer OurBigBook.com
Pea seed respirometry
Words: 274
Respirometer OurBigBook.com
The University of Oklahoma K20 Center's handout describes three sealed vial-and-pipette respirometers in each temperature bath: soaked, germinating peas; nongerminating peas plus inert plastic beads; and beads alone. Displaced water establishes equal occupied volumes. Absorbent cotton holds potassium hydroxide, which removes carbon dioxide; nonabsorbent cotton separates it from the peas. The source equilibrates the vials before submersion and again before the initial reading. Colored water makes the boundary visible in each calibrated pipette. Readers then record positions every five minutes for twenty minutes.[ref]
Bath temperature, vial position and seal integrity matter. The beads-only respirometer detects common temperature or atmospheric pressure drift; its change is subtracted from each pea reading. Nongerminating peas provide a biological comparison, not an assumption of zero cellular respiration. A larger corrected uptake slope for germinating peas would support greater molecular oxygen consumption by that sample under the tested conditions.[ref]
Equal displaced volumes help match the gas spaces; they do not establish equal living mass or equal developmental state. Comparing uptake per seed and uptake per dry mass asks different questions. Leaks, incomplete carbon dioxide absorption, gas dissolution and changing water-vapour contributions can distort the respirometer inference. A blank correction cannot repair a sample-specific leak. These are consequences of the respirometer gas balance, rather than measurements reported in the handout.
Respirometer gas balance
Words: 322 Articles: 1
Respirometer OurBigBook.com
For an original idealized mathematical model, let nO2​​(t) be the amount of substance of molecular oxygen consumed since the initial reading and nCO2​​(t) the carbon dioxide produced. Suppose a fraction f of that carbon dioxide is removed from the gas, all other gas inventories remain fixed, and temperature T and gas pressure P stay constant. The ideal gas law gives the positive gas contraction
D(t)=V(0)−V(t)=PRT​[nO2​​(t)−(1−f)nCO2​​(t)],
(24)
where R is the molar gas constant and V the gas volume. With complete absorption, f=1, the contraction reflects molecular oxygen uptake regardless of the amount of carbon dioxide made. For a uniform pipette bore of area A, an inward boundary displacement x gives D=Ax. A graduated pipette can instead supply the displaced volume directly.
Let Ds​ denote sample contraction and Db​ the matched blank contraction. Define Dcorr​=Ds​−Db​ with both taken relative to their own initial readings. Under the preceding assumptions,
nO2​​(t)≃RTPDcorr​(t)​,rO2​​=RTP​t2​−t1​Dcorr​(t2​)−Dcorr​(t1​)​.
(25)
The slope of corrected volume against time estimates uptake over the chosen interval. The approximate sign acknowledges that a liquid boundary also responds to hydrostatic and capillary pressure, while the gas can exchange water vapour. A fixed-volume apparatus would instead show a pressure decrease; its ideal conversion is nO2​​≃V(P(0)−P(t))/(RT) after complete absorption and appropriate blank correction.
The ideal gas law also exposes drift without any biology: for fixed gas inventory, V∝T/P. A one-percent rise in absolute temperature at fixed pressure produces a one-percent expansion. Matching the initial gas spaces makes such common changes easier to subtract. Subtracting unmatched blanks can leave a physical signal that looks biological.
Respiratory quotient (RQ=nCO2​​/nO2​​)
Words: 89
Respirometer gas balance OurBigBook.com
The respiratory quotient compares carbon dioxide production with molecular oxygen consumption over the same interval. Complete glucose oxidation in the net equation above gives RQ=6/6=1. In the ideal respirometer gas balance with no absorber, f=0, that conversion gives D=0: substantial cellular respiration can occur without any net gas contraction. A zero contraction therefore does not by itself demonstrate zero metabolism.
Other fuels, incomplete conversion and concurrent synthesis can alter the ratio. Absorber-based respirometry isolates molecular oxygen uptake by deliberately removing the other gas signal; it cannot independently determine the respiratory quotient or identify glucose as the consumed fuel. Separate carbon dioxide measurement would supply the missing account.

Evolution

Words: 4k Articles: 168
Biology OurBigBook.com
Evolution is descent with inherited modification. Within a population, changes in allele frequencies provide a precise genetic description; over longer histories, branching descent connects populations through common descent. An individual growing larger is biological development, whereas an inherited variant becoming more frequent across generations is evolution. See UC Museum of Paleontology: the definition of evolution.
Mutation supplies new alleles, genetic recombination reshuffles inherited material, natural selection favors variants with greater reproductive contribution in a specified environment, and genetic drift changes frequencies through chance. Gene flow moves variants between populations. Consequently, an increasing allele frequency alone does not identify natural selection. See Clark, Douglas and Choi, Biology 2e: population genetics.
Evidence includes ordered fossils, shared inherited structures and similarities in DNA; phylogenetics uses such observations to infer relationships. A phylogenetic tree is an inferred historical account, with uncertainty about particular branches. See Clark, Douglas and Choi, Biology 2e: evidence of evolution. Evidence also comes from experiments: Blount, Borland and Lenski reported an Escherichia coli lineage able to use citrate with oxygen present by 31,500 generations, and tested historical dependence by replaying evolution from stored ancestors. See Blount, Borland and Lenski, 2008: original experimental report. Such observations constrain explanations; no single frequency equation captures every evolutionary process.

Dietary divergence and mating isolation in Drosophila pseudoobscura
Words: 241
Reproductive isolation OurBigBook.com
The 1989 experiment used eight Drosophila pseudoobscura biological populations from one Bryce Canyon population: four maintained on starch medium, four on maltose, in cages at 25∘C. Testing began about a year after establishment. [ref]
Before testing, flies spent one generation on cornmeal–molasses–agar. Virgins aged 3–6 days entered multiple-choice chambers: twelve females from each population, followed by males from both populations introduced nearly simultaneously without anesthesia. Observers scored matings for 60–90 minutes under bright indirect lighting. One group's right wing tips were clipped for identification, with clipping reversed between replicates. [ref]
All sixteen cross-diet comparisons had positive mating assortment contrasts; eleven departed significantly from random mating. Same-diet comparisons did not show significant departures. Common-medium rearing addressed immediate diet conditioning; same-diet controls addressed separation and establishment population bottlenecks. Mate choice was not the selection target; the biological populations were maintained separately. The result supports partial premating isolation accompanying dietary divergence, not completed speciation. [ref]
The causal inference remains limited. A negative same-diet hypothesis test does not prove zero reproductive isolation. One generation under common conditions does not exclude every persistent environmental influence. The chamber readout alone cannot identify a particular gene, establish offspring fertility, or predict gene flow after sustained contact in nature. Further experiments would need to target those questions separately.
Mating assortment contrast (I=(Nsame​−Ncross​)/N)
Words: 147
Reproductive isolation OurBigBook.com
For observed pairings between two labels A,B, let Nsame​=NAA​+NBB​ and Ncross​=NAB​+NBA​, where the first label denotes the female's group and the second the male's. A mating assortment contrast is
I=NNsame​−Ncross​​,N=Nsame​+Ncross​>0.
(26)
It lies between −1 and 1. Positive I describes an excess of same-label pairings over cross-label pairings; whether that is evidence of assortative mating depends on the null mathematical model and the assay. The four counts form a contingency table.
Here is an original scope check. Suppose independently paired females and males have probabilities pf​,pm​ of carrying label A. Then
qsame​=pf​pm​+(1−pf​)(1−pm​),E[I]=2qsame​−1.
(27)
With pf​=pm​=1/2, the expected value is zero. With pf​=pm​=4/5, it is 9/25=0.36, despite pairing being independent of label. This counterexample concerns unequal pool composition; it does not replace the group introductions and contingency table tests in the dietary divergence and mating isolation in Drosophila pseudoobscura experiment. Even with balanced pools, finite observed samples fluctuate: a positive I alone is not a hypothesis test, much less a universal species boundary.

Natural selection

Words: 1k Articles: 39
Evolution OurBigBook.com
Natural selection involves systematic differences in expected reproductive success associated with variation in phenotype. For a continuing evolutionary response, the relevant variation must be inherited: offspring must tend to preserve the differences being favored. Actual offspring counts also fluctuate by chance, producing genetic drift. Survival matters insofar as it affects contribution to future generations. Genotype fitness is therefore contextual, depending on environment and the life cycle being counted, rather than simply measuring strength or longevity. See Clark, Douglas and Choi, Biology 2e: population evolution.
In chapter IV of his 1859 book, Darwin explained natural selection through preservation of favorable variations and greater chances of survival and reproduction. See Darwin, On the Origin of Species, first edition, chapter IV. The beautiful consequence is cumulative change without foresight: inherited differences are filtered repeatedly by present conditions. Natural selection neither generates a needed mutation on demand nor guarantees progress toward a predetermined goal.

p′=pmA​+(1−p)mB​pmA​​=wp+(1−p)wp​.
(28)
The denominator is mean relative genotype fitness. For w=1.2 and p0​=0.2, p1​=0.24/1.04=3/13≈0.23077. Equivalently, 200 A and 800 B parents with mA​=1.2,mB​=1 contribute expected counts 240 and 800. Fractional per-parent expected values are averages, not literal fractional offspring. The ratio of these expectations is a deterministic approximation, not generally the expectation of a random ratio.
The odds multiply particularly simply:
1−pt+1​pt+1​​=w1−pt​pt​​,pt​=1−p0​+wtp0​wtp0​​.
(29)
Thus p10​≈0.60753: repeated modest advantage can substantially change composition. For w>1 and 0<p<1, p′−p=(w−1)p(1−p)/(1+(w−1)p)>0. The deterministic boundary p=0 remains unchanged: natural selection needs existing variation.
A distinct stochastic extension fixes N offspring and samples their types independently using a binomial distribution: K∼Binomial(N,q), where q=wp/(wp+1−p), then p′=K/N. Its conditional expected value is q and conditional variance is q(1−q)/N. With w=1, the conditional expected value remains p, yet realized frequencies wander through genetic drift. With w>1, genetic drift can still lower p or lose A entirely. Over several generations, the deterministic curve need not equal the mean stochastic trajectory, because the recurrence is nonlinear.

For an original counting example, stipulate a plant with 2n=14 chromosomes and the common two-polar-nucleus arrangement. Each haploid sperm and ovum contributes n=7. The zygote therefore has 7+7=14 chromosomes, while the initiating endosperm cell nucleus has 7+7+7=21. The maternal seed coat remains derived from 2n=14 plant tissue; the whole seed has no single uniform chromosome count. This is bookkeeping for a stipulated example, not identification of a particular species. It follows by counting the chromosome sets entering each fusion, rather than assigning one count to everything enclosed by a seed coat.

Pollen tube germination assay
Words: 492
Pollen tube OurBigBook.com
A pollen tube germination assay makes tube emergence visible outside a flower. The published Practical Biology experiment, Observing the growth of pollen tubes (Practical Biology), Technical note 3, lists florist lilies among successful materials without specifying a species. Record the actual identification; success with one sample cannot establish a universal growth rate.[ref]
Pearson's Core practical 4: Investigate the effect of sucrose concentration on pollen tube growth by Pearson Education Ltd, Teacher sheet, pp. 1–2, describes an inspectable experiment. Mix equal volumes of sucrose solution and mineral-salt medium on clean cavity slides. Dust in pollen from mature anthers with a mounted needle, record the addition time, and incubate without coverslips in covered dishes containing wet filter paper. The moist chamber reduces drying; the uncovered drops avoid oxygen limitation. Brief observations with an optical microscope at 100×, using an eyepiece graticule calibrated against a stage micrometer, reveal tube emergence and length. Return slides to the chambers and switch off the lamp between observations to reduce heating and drying. For comparisons of sucrose concentration, use the same flower across treatments to control maturity, then repeat with other flowers.[ref]
An additional proposed experimental design check is a medium-only slide: it tests whether debris is being mistaken for pollen tubes. Compare matched pollen samples at different final sucrose concentrations, keeping temperature, elapsed time and observation rules fixed. A sample known to produce pollen tubes in a previously successful medium would test whether an apparent failure comes from handling or the tested condition. These controls are questions to test, not guaranteed outcomes. A negative result cannot distinguish dead pollen from an unsuitable medium without further comparisons.
Two original calculations clarify the readout. First, take 0.40mL of 0.80molL−1 sucrose solution and 0.40mL of sucrose-free medium. Assuming additive volumes, conservation of the amount of substance gives
cfinal​=Vstock​+Vmedium​cstock​Vstock​​=0.40molL−1.
(30)
This dilution also halves the medium's original component concentrations. Label the final molar concentration, not the starting bottle.
Second, stipulate a toy field containing 40 pollen grains, of which 12 have emerged pollen tubes. Its emergence fraction is 12/40=0.30. If those twelve pollen tubes have total measured length 960μm, their arithmetic mean length is 80μm. Assigning length zero to the other grains instead gives 960/40=24μm per grain. These invented numbers show why emergence fraction and mean length among emerged tubes answer different questions. Specify the denominator and the emergence criterion before counting, and avoid selecting only conspicuous long pollen tubes.
Tube emergence in a drop demonstrates growth under that medium's conditions. It observes no stigma interaction, passage through a style, delivery into an ovule, gamete fusion, or seed development. Thus a positive pollen tube germination assay does not demonstrate successful fertilization in a living flower. Its beauty is making one otherwise hidden part of sexual reproduction directly observable.[ref]

Gel electrophoresis

Biology OurBigBook.com
Separation of charged molecules through a gel in an electric field. Denaturing conditions suppress folded structures, helping compare RNA lengths; matching migration alone does not establish an identical nucleotide sequence or identical covalent bonds. In the ribozyme experiments, labelled RNA was detected after separation by exposing photographic film.
In DNA agarose gel electrophoresis, the backbone phosphate groups carry negative electric charge under the usual mildly alkaline buffer solution conditions. DNA therefore moves toward the positive anode, away from the negative cathode.[ref]
The electric field points the other way: the electric force F=qE reverses direction when q<0. The apparatus is driven by an external source of electric potential difference; the positive anode convention here belongs to that operating mode. Direction follows electric charge, so it is not a rule that all molecules move toward the same electrode.
The useful result is a spatial comparison: a mixture becomes separated gel bands, which can be compared with a DNA ladder or recovered for subsequent analysis. Agarose gel electrophoresis of linear double-stranded DNA, gel electrophoresis of denatured RNA, and SDS-PAGE of proteins use different conditions to make migration informative about chain size. An electric field supplies motion; the gel supplies a porous obstacle course.

A binding assay that detects a change in electrophoretic mobility when a ligand associates with a labelled target, such as an RNA–protein complex. A concentration series and competition controls help distinguish specific binding from aggregation or non-specific retention.

Gel band

Words: 197
Gel electrophoresis OurBigBook.com
A gel band is a localized population of stained or otherwise detected molecules with sufficiently similar migration in one sample lane. One visible gel band need not contain only one nucleotide sequence. Two different linear DNA fragments of 375 base pairs can occupy the same unresolved gel band; equal migration supplies size evidence under suitable conditions, not a sequence determination.
Fluorescence from a bound stain can support an estimate of DNA quantity, but suitable staining and detector response matter.[ref]
For a quantitative model with equal staining response per unit mass, background-subtracted, integrated fluorescence I satisfies I=km. This requires an unsaturated detector and a common proportionality constant k; visual peak brightness alone does not supply I.
The amount of substance is n=m/M, where M is molar mass. For double-stranded DNA with approximately equal average mass per base pair, M is proportional to length L, so n is proportional to I/L. In a constructed example, equal integrated signals from 250-base pair and 1000-base pair gel bands imply approximately equal masses but four times as many short DNA molecules. Conversely, equal numbers of those DNA molecules would give about four times the signal for the longer fragments in this model. Neither conclusion follows from darkness in a schematic drawing.

Agarose gel electrophoresis

Words: 620 Articles: 2
Gel electrophoresis OurBigBook.com
Agarose gel electrophoresis uses a porous agarose polymer network. For linear double-stranded DNA within a suitable separation range, shorter fragments generally move farther in a fixed run. Raising the agarose concentration changes the mesh and the range of sizes that can be resolved.[ref] A compact circular DNA molecule need not migrate like linear DNA of the same length: geometry affects passage through the mesh.[ref]
A concrete laboratory example is Addgene's documented DNA separation protocol. Its standard 1% gel contains 1 g of agarose in 100 mL of TAE buffer. Dissolved agarose sets in a casting tray around a comb; removing the comb leaves sample wells. The gel is covered with the same buffer solution in a box connected to a voltage source. Loading buffer contains glycerol to increase sample density and a tracking dye to show run progress. A DNA ladder occupies a separate lane beside the samples. With wells near the negative cathode, DNA migrates toward the positive anode. After separation, bound stain makes the DNA visible by fluorescence under a UV transilluminator. The DNA ladder supplies the size reference; the tracking dye monitors migration but does not identify sample DNA.[ref]
In the manufacturer's controlled comparison, the same DNA ladder runs in 1%, 2%, and 3% agarose gels with the same run time and other stated conditions. The changed gel band spacing shows why a calibration belongs to its particular gel conditions, rather than establishing a universal distance law.[ref]
In interpreting an unknown sample, a blank lane tests for detectable background or carryover in that blank, while the DNA ladder checks migration and detection of its known fragments. An empty sample lane cannot by itself distinguish absent DNA from unsuccessful loading or insufficient detection. These controls answer different questions; neither makes matching migration a proof of matching nucleotide sequence.

DNA ladder

Words: 50
Agarose gel electrophoresis OurBigBook.com
A DNA ladder contains DNA fragments of known lengths in base pairs. Its gel bands supply size references. Match the sample's strandedness and shape, and use the specified lengths for that DNA ladder. A size reference need not provide a quantitative mass standard.[ref]

Gel electrophoresis size calibration (d=a−blog10​(L/L0​))

Words: 233
Agarose gel electrophoresis OurBigBook.com
A gel electrophoresis size calibration relates migration distance to known fragment lengths on the same gel. Here is an explicitly chosen model for linear double-stranded DNA, not measured data or a universal law. Let L be the numerical length in base pairs and d the numerical migration distance in millimetres from the wells:
d=55−12log10​(L/100).
(31)
The logarithm has a dimensionless argument: L/100 is the length divided by 100 base pairs. The chosen DNA ladder fragments L=100,250,500,1000 give d=55.00,50.22,46.61,43.00, respectively. The gel bands therefore appear in the reverse order of length along the direction of migration.
To invert the calibration, rearrange the logarithm:
L=10010(55−d)/12.
(32)
Our chosen unknown L=375 gives d=48.1116248…, between the 250-base pair and 500-base pair references. Inserting that distance into the inverse recovers 375; retaining only d=48.11 gives about 375.12 base pairs. The extra digits reflect rounding in this model, not the resolving power of a real gel.
For linear interpolation between those two reference gel bands, use the logarithm of length. Here the fraction of the distance from the 500-base pair reference toward the 250-base pair reference is t=log10​(500/375)/log10​2≈0.4150, giving L=500(250/500)t=375. Direct linear interpolation of lengths instead gives approximately 396.24 base pairs. This difference explains why the choice of calibration coordinates matters. A real calibration must be checked over its usable range; folded RNA or circular DNA does not automatically share the linear double-stranded DNA calibration.

Medicine OurBigBook.com

Survival of a subpopulation during bactericidal exposure while the broader population remains susceptible. Regrown survivors can recover the original susceptibility; persistence is not synonymous with every persistent infection.

Minimum inhibitory concentration

Words: 27
Antibiotic OurBigBook.com
The lowest tested antimicrobial concentration preventing defined visible growth under specified conditions. It measures an organism-level response, not just the catalytic efficiency of an isolated resistance enzyme.

Antibiotic OurBigBook.com
Antibiotic resistance is the ability of a microorganism to grow or survive under specified antibiotic exposure that inhibits a susceptible comparison.
